Herodian’s -σος Accent Toy (disyllables)

Type a Greek word in -σος (e.g. νῆσος, Κνωσός, Παισός). The toy guesses whether it should be barytone (accent not on the last syllable) or oxytone (accent on the last syllable) using simplified rules from the passage.

Mini game: “Spot the penult”

Click the penult vowel group the toy thinks matters (η / ω / long ι/υ / diphthong). Then reveal.

—
What rules are being mimicked?
  • η in penult (…ησος) → usually barytone (e.g. νῆσος, Βῆσος).
  • ω in penult and feminine → oxytone (toy can’t know gender; it just flags the pattern and notes exceptions like Σῶσος, Κρῶσος).
  • long ι/υ in penult (…ῖσος/…ῦσος) → usually barytone for proper names etc. (Ἶσος, Κῖσος, Νῦσος).
  • diphthong in penult (αι/ει/οι/υι/αυ/ευ/ου/ηυ/ωυ) → often oxytone when adjectival or a place-name (Παισός, Πραισός, Μαυσός).

This is a playful heuristic, not a full accentuation engine.

original.english_translation: Disyllables in -σος with η in the penult are barytone: νῆσος, and Νῆσος, an Iberian city. But νῆσος is exceptional with respect to gender; for the others are masculine: Βῆσος, Μνῆσος, Ῥῆσος, Κτῆσος, Θῆσος, Δρῆσος, Κῆσος, the name of a river. Disyllabic feminines in -σος with ω in the penult are oxytone: κρωσός, “the water-jar,” Κνωσός, “who held Κνωσόν” (Β 646), with one σ, though Tryphon writes it with two; Ῥωσός, a city of Cilicia. However, Σῶσος, from σώσω, is barytone, and likewise Κρῶσος, masculine. Disyllabic masculine monogender nouns in -σος with a long diphthongal penult are barytone: Ἶσος, the proper name; Κῖσος; Κρῖσος, the proper name; Πῖσος, the proper name, from which also Πῖσα, the city; Νῖσος, son of Pandion, from whom Νίσαια; Νῦσος, a river; Τρῦσος, a river; κῦσος. But Λισός, a small town of Crete, is oxytone, as are Βρυσός, the harbor, and Μυσός, an ethnic, and τρυσός, ῥυσός as adjectives, and χρυσός, the only appellative disyllable in -υσος. Disyllables in -σος with a diphthong in the penult are oxytone when they are adjectival or denote a city: Παισός, a city in the Troad. Homer: “who dwelt in Παισῷ, rich in possessions” (Il. Ε 612), and elsewhere “the people of Ἀπαισοῦ” (Il. Β 828). Παισός is said to be from the fact that the Argo, putting in there, struck (παῖσαι) and came close. Παισός, and with addition of α, Ἀπαισός, just as Ἄταρνα, a city, and Τάρνα. Homer: “who was from Τάρνη of the rich-soiled land” (Il. Ε 44). There is also in Daunia a city Παισός near Ἀργύριππα. Λουσός and Λουσοί, a city of Arcadia, where Melampus bathed the daughters of Proetus and stopped their madness; it is also said as Λοῦσα in the neuter. Πραισός, a city. Μαυσός, a village of Corinth. candidate.html:
Herodian’s -σος Passage Explorer

Look up a cited Greek word in -σος (e.g. νῆσος, Σῶσος, χρυσός). Compare the passage’s accent groups and named exceptions. Unlisted words receive no inferred accent.

Mini game: “Spot the penult”

Choose the penult vowel group in the cited example (η / ω / ι/υ / diphthong). Then reveal.

—
What rules are being mimicked?
  • η in penult (…ησος) → usually barytone (e.g. νῆσος, Βῆσος).
  • ω in penult and feminine → oxytone (the cited feminine group is oxytone; Σῶσος and masculine Κρῶσος are barytone exceptions).
  • long ι/υ in penult → barytone in the cited masculine monogender group (Ἶσος, Κῖσος, Νῦσος).
  • diphthong in penult (αι/ει/οι/υι/αυ/ευ/ου/ηυ/ωυ) → often oxytone when adjectival or a place-name (Παισός, Πραισός, Μαυσός).

This explorer returns cited forms only. It cannot infer vowel length or gender from unaccented spelling. The passage specifies long ι/υ for its masculine group.

original.english_translation: Disyllables in -σος with η in the penult are barytone: νῆσος, and Νῆσος, an Iberian city. But νῆσος is exceptional with respect to gender; for the others are masculine: Βῆσος, Μνῆσος, Ῥῆσος, Κτῆσος, Θῆσος, Δρῆσος, Κῆσος, the name of a river. Disyllabic feminines in -σος with ω in the penult are oxytone: κρωσός, “the water-jar,” Κνωσός, “who held Κνωσόν” (Β 646), with one σ, though Tryphon writes it with two; Ῥωσός, a city of Cilicia. However, Σῶσος, from σώσω, is barytone, and likewise Κρῶσος, masculine. Disyllabic masculine monogender nouns in -σος with a long diphthongal penult are barytone: Ἶσος, the proper name; Κῖσος; Κρῖσος, the proper name; Πῖσος, the proper name, from which also Πῖσα, the city; Νῖσος, son of Pandion, from whom Νίσαια; Νῦσος, a river; Τρῦσος, a river; κῦσος. But Λισός, a small town of Crete, is oxytone, as are Βρυσός, the harbor, and Μυσός, an ethnic, and τρυσός, ῥυσός as adjectives, and χρυσός, the only appellative disyllable in -υσος. Disyllables in -σος with a diphthong in the penult are oxytone when they are adjectival or denote a city: Παισός, a city in the Troad. Homer: “who dwelt in Παισῷ, rich in possessions” (Il. Ε 612), and elsewhere “the people of Ἀπαισοῦ” (Il. Β 828). Παισός is said to be from the fact that the Argo, putting in there, struck (παῖσαι) and came close. Παισός, and with addition of α, Ἀπαισός, just as Ἄταρνα, a city, and Τάρνα. Homer: “who was from Τάρνη of the rich-soiled land” (Il. Ε 44). There is also in Daunia a city Παισός near Ἀργύριππα. Λουσός and Λουσοί, a city of Arcadia, where Melampus bathed the daughters of Proetus and stopped their madness; it is also said as Λοῦσα in the neuter. Πραισός, a city. Μαυσός, a village of Corinth. Theopompus in the thirty-second book. And the adjectival ones too,
original.gadget_html:
Herodian’s -σος Accent Toy (disyllables)

Type a Greek word in -σος (e.g. νῆσος, Κνωσός, Παισός). The toy guesses whether it should be barytone (accent not on the last syllable) or oxytone (accent on the last syllable) using simplified rules from the passage.

Mini game: “Spot the penult”

Click the penult vowel group the toy thinks matters (η / ω / long ι/υ / diphthong). Then reveal.

—
What rules are being mimicked?
  • η in penult (…ησος) → usually barytone (e.g. νῆσος, Βῆσος).
  • ω in penult and feminine → oxytone (toy can’t know gender; it just flags the pattern and notes exceptions like Σῶσος, Κρῶσος).
  • long ι/υ in penult (…ῖσος/…ῦσος) → usually barytone for proper names etc. (Ἶσος, Κῖσος, Νῦσος).
  • diphthong in penult (αι/ει/οι/υι/αυ/ευ/ου/ηυ/ωυ) → often oxytone when adjectival or a place-name (Παισός, Πραισός, Μαυσός).

This is a playful heuristic, not a full accentuation engine.

Ῥωσός πόλις Κιλικίας. τὸ μέντοι Σῶσος ἀπὸ τοῦ σώσω βαρύνεται, καὶ τὸ Κρῶσος ὁμοίως ἀρσενικόν. Τὰ εἰς 'σος' δισύλλαβα ἀρσενικὰ μονογενῆ παραληγόμενα διχρόνῳ ἐκτεταμένῳ βαρύνεται, Ἶσος τὸ κύριον, Κῖσος, Κρῖσος τὸ κύριον, Πῖσος τὸ κύριον, ἀφ´ οὗ καὶ Πῖσα ἡ πόλις.
